items.title: Hindu philosophy teaches the unity of atman and Brahman
items.claim: What is the relationship between atman and Brahman in Vedantic Hinduism?

options.text: They are completely separate — the soul and a creator god

The Upanishads teach that atman (the individual self) and Brahman (ultimate reality) are one — 'tat tvam asi' ('that thou art', Chandogya Upanishad). Different Vedanta schools interpret the relationship variously (non-dual, qualified non-dual, dualist)
Atman is illusion; only Brahman is real, with no relation between them
Brahman is a god subordinate to atman

items.reveal:
The Mahavakyas ('great sayings') include 'tat tvam asi' (Chandogya 6.8.7), 'aham brahmasmi' (Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10) and 'ayam atma brahma' (Mandukya 2).

Shankara (8th century CE) developed Advaita Vedanta — non-duality: atman is identical to Brahman; perceived multiplicity is maya (illusion).

Ramanuja (11th-12th century) taught Vishishtadvaita — qualified non-duality: atman is a real attribute of Brahman but distinct. Madhva (13th century) taught Dvaita — full dualism: souls and God are eternally distinct.

All three schools are valid orthodox Vedantic positions.
items.why: Hindu philosophy of self is sophisticated. Treating Hinduism as 'just polytheism' misses the metaphysical core that has shaped Indian thought for over two millennia.

items.title: Jihad has greater and lesser meanings in classical Islam
items.claim: What is the greater/lesser jihad distinction?

options.text: Both refer only to armed warfare

A widely cited hadith distinguishes lesser jihad (armed struggle in defence of the community) from greater jihad (inner struggle against one's own ego); the hadith's authenticity is debated but the inner-struggle understanding is found in independent Sufi and mainstream piety traditions
Jihad refers only to economic struggle

items.reveal:
The Arabic root j-h-d means 'to strive, to exert effort'. The greater/lesser distinction is attributed to a hadith reported by al-Bayhaqi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi: 'We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the jihad against the self.'

Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) and some modern scholars question the hadith's chain of authentication. But the inner-struggle theme appears widely in Sufi writing and is not dependent on the hadith alone.

Classical Islamic law (fiqh) regulates armed jihad with conditions on declaration, conduct, and protection of non-combatants — distinct from later extremist appropriations of the term.
items.why: A word picked up by 21st-century media can carry meanings that don't match its theological tradition. 'Jihad' in classical Islam is far more various than its English-language press usage.

items.title: The Khalsa was founded at Vaisakhi 1699
items.claim: What did Guru Gobind Singh establish in 1699?

options.text: A new Sikh state in northern India
The Khalsa (the 'pure') — a community of initiated Sikhs marked by the Five Ks (Kesh, Kara, Kanga, Kachera, Kirpan), open to all castes and gender
A revised version of the Guru Granth Sahib
A peace treaty with the Mughal Empire

items.reveal:
At Anandpur on Vaisakhi (April) 1699, Guru Gobind Singh called for volunteers willing to die for the faith. The Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones) came forward, were initiated with amrit (sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword), and were then themselves used to initiate Gobind Singh.

The Five Ks: Kesh (uncut hair, including the dastaar turban), Kara (steel bracelet), Kanga (wooden comb), Kachera (cotton undergarment), Kirpan (small sword).

The Khalsa took the surname Singh (lion) for men and Kaur (princess) for women — symbolically equalising caste and gender.
items.why: Sikh identity has visible bodily markers that emerged from a specific 1699 event with named participants. The Five Ks are not vague cultural symbols but coded responses to Mughal-era persecution and caste hierarchy.
